core.text: A reason for the main clause can be given by **cum + subjunctive meaning 'since' (or, with tamen, 'although')**: *plōrō, cum mortua sit* — I weep, since she is dead. Unlike the story-telling *cum*, it works in any tense: the present subjunctive (the 'may / let' form: veniat = let him come, may he come) after a present main verb, the imperfect after a past one. With *tamen* (nevertheless) in the main clause it is a concession: *cum dīves sit, tamen miser est* — although he is rich, he is unhappy. Latin name: *cum causāle et concessīvum*.
*Since* and *because* give a reason; *although* admits something and then goes against it. One Latin word does both jobs; the subjunctive marks it.
cum + subjunctive = since / because; cum … tamen = although; quippe quī + subjunctive = 'as one who', another way of giving a reason.

invented.la: Cum pecūniam nōn habeam, pānem emere nōn possum.
invented.en: Since I have no money, I cannot buy bread.

invented.la: Cum servus sit, tamen līber esse vidētur.
invented.en: Although he is a slave, he nevertheless seems free.

core.text: Story *cum* appears only with the imperfect or pluperfect in a past narrative and tells you *when*. If the cum verb is present or perfect subjunctive, or the clause answers *why*, it is causal. Test by translating 'since': if it fits, causal.

more.text: Also easy to confuse: *cum* followed by a noun in the ablative (the 'by/with/from' form) is just 'with' — *cum Dāvō ambulat*. A causal *cum* has its own verb in the subjunctive.

The learner's notes: the causal subjunctive is usually introduced by *cum*, 'effectively making it mean since or because' — *audīmus, cum ipse loquāris* (we listen, because you yourself are speaking), *ambulāmus, cum nōn sit nōbīs equus*. A relative clause can do it too, often with *quippe* to make it clear: *sitiō quippe quī nūllam aquam habeam* — I am thirsty, as one who has no water.

For a finished reason after a present verb the perfect subjunctive is used (Week 10): *nōn possum exīre cum aliquis portam clauserit* — I cannot go out since someone has shut the gate; after a past verb the pluperfect: *nōn poteram exīre cum … clausisset*. *cum* + indicative still means plain 'when(ever)': *gaudeō cum dē līberīs cōgitō*. Ørberg writes 'although' with *quamquam* + indicative (*quamquam valdē dolēbat, tamen …*); *cum … tamen* is the subjunctive version of the same idea.
